summary:
Recommendation: move the wordpress MySQL database to three purpose-built AWS services in three waves, with every target schema designed. Wave 1 moves it to Aurora MySQL, which keeps 66.3% of the queries on the same engine family. Wave 2 puts ElastiCache in front of 38 hot reads, 82.1% of calls. Wave 3 moves 33.7% of the queries to DynamoDB. The projected cost of the full modernization is $1,300 per month at AWS Price List on-demand prices for us-east-1, retrieved 2026-11-04. No current cost was collected for the source database, so the plan claims no saving against it.

Risk: overall risk is medium, with 9 open medium-severity risks. Two drive it, both in wave 3. Reads on Aurora MySQL use copies that change data capture (CDC) keeps current from DynamoDB, so test that replication. A group of queries was settled by a close score between Aurora MySQL and DynamoDB, so confirm where those queries run before wave 3 starts.

Decision: approve wave 1. It moves the database 1:1 to Aurora MySQL, the same engine family as MySQL, and keeps its current data model. The cutover is your responsibility. Approving wave 1 accepts its 2 design review warnings, listed in the roadmap. Approving wave 2 accepts its 3 design review warnings, listed in the roadmap. Approving wave 3 accepts its 4 design review warnings, listed in the roadmap.

Schema design produced 70 target objects: 163 queries in 83 query groups; 190 in-scope access patterns (Aurora MySQL: 22 target tables, 108 in-scope access patterns; DynamoDB: 17 target tables, 48 in-scope access patterns; ElastiCache: 31 key designs, 34 in-scope access patterns). Other targets evaluated: DocumentDB (consolidated into Aurora MySQL by the reality check), OpenSearch (consolidated into Aurora MySQL by the reality check).

assumptions: On-demand capacity mode for all target databases
Does not include data transfer, backups, or global tables
Reads the cache layer fronts are also billed on their owner engines, as if every one missed the cache (conservative)
27 source tables no in-scope query reads (<0.01 GB) are stored on Aurora MySQL, where wave 1 moves them

The DynamoDB figure includes $122.12/mo for the design's 5 global secondary indexes at on-demand prices: $0.05 of storage (each index's item count times its projected item size plus 100 bytes of index overhead per item) and $122.07 of index writes (one for each put or delete whose item may set the index's keys, two for an update that changes an index key or does not say what it changes, one for an update that changes only a projected attribute, billed at the standard rate per 1 KB of the projected item, on average load with the collected rows per call, an average of exactly zero counted as one row). Index reads are not added, since each is one of its query's reads and already priced, and the free tier is left out
DynamoDB reads are priced eventually consistent, except transactions, which are priced at transactional rates.

risks.description: [dynamodb] Wave 3: 104 queries read 20 tables on an engine that does not own them. 103 of them read a copy of 19 tables that CDC keeps current from DynamoDB across 1 engine pair, so a read there can miss a recent write. The other table is written by no captured query; CDC keeps its copy current too, and the copy changes only when something outside the captured workload writes the table.
risks.mitigation: Before Wave 3 starts, set up CDC for each engine pair the sources of truth section lists, and send any read that must see its own write to its source of truth; set up CDC for the table no captured query writes, and check whether anything outside the captured workload writes it. Compare the row counts on both sides. See the Wave 3 gate in the roadmap.

risks.description: [dynamodb] Wave 3: 29 queries were decided by less than 5 points, and 5 more were exact ties a routing rule settled: Aurora MySQL keeps 19 close calls and 5 ties over DynamoDB; DynamoDB takes 10 close calls over Aurora MySQL. A small change in the scores moves them.
risks.mitigation: Confirm the engine for these queries in the assignment review before Wave 3 starts, using the close calls section; move any that fit the runner-up better.

risks.description: [elasticache] 1 read the plan meant to cache was dropped from the cache layer and goes to Aurora MySQL uncached.
risks.mitigation: Load-test these reads on Aurora MySQL without the cache, or add a cache design that serves them. See the Wave 2 gate in the roadmap.

risks.description: [elasticache] The cache design marks 1 pattern unsupported; the engineering report lists each one with its workaround under Target schemas by engine.
details: unsupported pattern: Query `aa03c203` (`FOUND_ROWS()`) reads no table: it returns the row count of the previous `SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS` query on the same database connection, so it has no cacheable key. Workaround: The query stays on its owner database. When the child id list of `EC-AP-22` comes from the cache, the application takes the total from that array's length and skips this call
risks.mitigation: Serve this pattern from its owner engine or add it to the cache design, as the design's workaround for each says. See the Wave 2 gate in the roadmap.

details: Capacity uses the measured request rates (peak not measured, so the peak factor is 1) and the measured average row sizes; the busiest key load is the `wp_posts` table's 54.6 read units per second in total, spread over 24,276 posts
Comments and their meta share one item collection in the `wp_comments` table keyed by comment_id, with sort keys COMMENT and META#{meta_key}#{meta_id}

ConsumerKeyIndex uses an INCLUDE projection of user_id, permissions, consumer_secret and nonces, which covers every column query `1794daed` returns, and leaves last_access out so the 85 updates per second of query `0452bed2` never write to the index

Customer items stay keyed by the surrogate customer_id (CUSTOMER#{customer_id}): the natural candidate user_id is unique but nullable, since guest customers have no WordPress account, so it cannot be the table key
DATETIME and TIMESTAMP columns become ISO 8601 strings, and the MySQL zero date '0000-00-00 00:00:00' is written as an absent attribute
DATETIME columns become ISO 8601 strings; the source default '0000-00-00 00:00:00' has no valid ISO form and is written as an empty string

Every table keeps the source's surrogate id in its key: no natural attribute in this part qualifies, since sku in wp_wc_product_meta_lookup is nullable and not unique, and the unique (term_id, taxonomy) pair of wp_term_taxonomy is not what its queries look up by (they read by term_taxonomy_id)

Large text columns stay inline: meta_value in wp_usermeta (144-byte average row) and in wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta (139 bytes), order_item_name (131 bytes), description in wp_term_taxonomy (3,495 bytes) and schedule and extended_args in wp_actionscheduler_actions (706 bytes) are all far below the 400 KB item limit; wp_termmeta has no rows to measure

MySQL generated option_id with AUTO_INCREMENT; the application now generates it as a 64-bit time-ordered id (timestamp, worker and sequence bits) and writes it with if_not_exists(option_id, :new_id) in the upsert, so an existing option keeps its id

No sentinel items are written for users: the source has no unique index besides the primary key on `wp_users` (user_email and user_login are non-unique indexes), so DynamoDB enforces uniqueness on user_id only

OptionsByAutoload lags the wp_options table until DynamoDB applies each write to it, so the autoload Query can return an option's previous value; a caller that must see the latest value reads the item with a strongly consistent GetItem on option_name

Order item meta rows are stored in the same item collection as their order item, keyed by order_item_id with sort keys ITEM and META#{meta_id}, because every meta write in scope (queries `2caa2be1` and `4b856e29`) addresses meta by order_item_id
Posts and their meta share one item collection in the `wp_posts` table keyed by post_id: the post is the item with sort key POST and each meta row an item with sort key META#{meta_key}#{meta_id}
REPLACE INTO wp_wc_product_meta_lookup (query `d72966f8`) becomes an unconditional PutItem on product_id, which replaces the whole item in one write where MySQL deletes and reinserts the row
Reads by an IN list of IDs (posts, comments, users) become BatchGetItem calls of up to 100 keys, and the comment meta read by an IN list of comment IDs becomes one Query per comment run in parallel

Term meta is keyed by term_id with meta_id as the sort key, and the KEYS_ONLY index TermMetaByTermAndKey (partition key term_id and meta_key, sort key meta_id) serves the meta_id lookup (query `ee386e4a`) and finds the items the key-scoped update (query `3c5c8a79`) changes

TermMetaByTermAndKey lags the wp_termmeta table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a caller that must see a meta row written in the same request reads the term's base items with a strongly consistent Query on term_id

The 2 tax rate classes share one constant partition key (tax_rate_class_scope = ALL) with tax_rate_class_id as the sort key, so query `329367a2` is one Query instead of a full table scan, and the application sorts the 2 items by name

The KEYS_ONLY index PostmetaByMetaId on meta_id serves the delete of post meta by meta_id (query `596b8fed`), which names no post_id; only META items carry meta_id, so post items stay out of the index

The UPDATE by option_name carries attribute_exists(option_name), so it changes only an option that exists, as the SQL UPDATE does, while the INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE becomes an unconditional UpdateItem that creates or overwrites

The `wp_woocommerce_api_keys` table stays keyed by key_id, and the consumer-key lookup of query `1794daed` runs on the ConsumerKeyIndex GSI, because the source's consumer_key index is not unique and a table key on it would let one PutItem overwrite another key's row

The auto-increment ids action_id, umeta_id, order_item_id and meta_id of order item meta are generated by the application on insert, and each new item's PutItem is conditional on the id not existing where a duplicate would overwrite a row

The auto-increment ids log_id, customer_id, key_id and permission_id are generated by the application, and the log insert of query `b05af520` carries attribute_not_exists(log_id) so a reused id fails instead of overwriting a log entry

The autoload read (query `413c99e4`) is served by the OptionsByAutoload index, partitioned on autoload with option_name as sort key and option_value projected, so one Query returns the about 249 autoloaded options without a Scan or a base-table fetch
The comment meta count by comment and meta key (query `0278ef63`) is a Query with Select=COUNT on the comment partition and the META#{meta_key}# prefix, with no counter item
The customer-by-user lookup of query `3b1641a7` is a strongly consistent GetItem on the user's sentinel item, which carries customer_id, so no GSI on user_id is needed

The long text columns (post_content, post_content_filtered, post_title, post_excerpt, to_ping, pinged, comment_content and both meta_value columns) stay inline: the measured average rows are 757 bytes for posts, 446 for comments and 151 for post meta, against the 400 KB item limit

The meta sort key META#{meta_key}#{meta_id} groups a post's or comment's meta by key; a NULL meta_key becomes an empty segment (META##{meta_id}), and the meta-by-comment read (query `65f7884e`) is sorted by meta_id in the application

The nonces LONGTEXT column of `wp_woocommerce_api_keys` stays inline as a string attribute: the table's measured avg_row_size_bytes is 52,429 against the 400 KB item limit, and the design counts the column at 1 KB
The post read by ID and post type (query `3440484f`) is a GetItem by post_id with the post_type check done in the application

The scheduled-action insert (query `7ead756f`) is an INSERT ... SELECT guarded by a subquery that tests only a bound value, so the application evaluates that guard and then writes a PutItem conditional on attribute_not_exists(action_id)
The source REPLACE INTO of queries `611079ff` and `ee8b8e21` becomes a Put of the whole CUSTOMER item, which replaces the previous version in place, inside the sentinel transaction

The source primary key option_id stays reachable through the KEYS_ONLY index OptionsById, so another part of the design that reads an option by its id finds its option_name with one Query and then reads the item

The source's AUTO_INCREMENT ids for posts, post meta, comments, comment meta and users are generated by the application, and each insert is a conditional PutItem that fails when the key already exists

The tables keep the source surrogate ids (post ID, comment ID, user ID) as partition keys: post_name, user_login and user_email have only non-unique indexes in the source, so none of them is proven unique enough to be a key

The unique user_id of `wp_wc_customer_lookup` is enforced with a USER_ID_SENTINEL item (USER#{user_id}) in the same item collection, written with the CUSTOMER item in one TransactWriteItems whose Put carries attribute_not_exists(customer_lookup_key) OR customer_id = :customer_id

The wp_options table is keyed on option_name instead of the surrogate option_id, because every in-scope read and write addresses an option by its name and option_name is unique, NOT NULL and has one distinct value per row (55,527)
User meta updates by user_id and meta_key (query `41b2f2d1`) are a Query on the user's partition with a filter on meta_key, then an UpdateItem per match, with no secondary index

`wp_woocommerce_downloadable_product_permissions` is keyed order_id plus permission_id and `wp_wc_reserved_stock` order_id plus product_id, so the key-scoped writes of queries `2264704d` and `77cd1ad7` find their items with a Query on order_id and then update or delete each item by key
option_value (LONGTEXT) stays inline in the item: the table's average row is 338 bytes against the 400 KB item limit
risks.mitigation: Review these trade-offs with the team that builds DynamoDB before Wave 3 starts, and test each one the application depends on.

risks.description: [elasticache] The ElastiCache schema design records 10 trade-offs to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
details: Each metadata table (post, user, order item, term, comment meta) is cached as one JSON array per parent id, read in full and deleted in full on any write to that parent
Every cached key is cleared by the application after the owner write commits, and every key carries a TTL as the fallback bound
IN-list queries (posts, post meta, user meta, order item meta, terms, comment meta) become one pipelined `GET` per id, because the per-entity hash tags put the ids in different slots
Lookups that return no row in most calls (option names at 0.31 rows a call, post titles and child posts at zero, post meta existence at 0.04) cache a miss marker with a 300-second TTL
The cached user rows hold password hashes and activation keys, and cached user meta holds session tokens, because the source queries return every column
The cached working set is about 300 MB across about 500,000 keys at full fill, the largest being post rows (about 100 MB) and post meta arrays (about 63 MB)
The object-to-terms joins are denormalized into one array per object and taxonomy, holding each term's id and name in name order
The related-products query (query `4b79d7a8`) is cached as its result list, keyed by a digest of its parameters, with expiry as its only invalidation

The slug check before a post save (query `fcfd82fa`) and the pending-action check before an action is scheduled (query `06584926`) are served from the cache, with the insert that changes each answer deleting its key
`FOUND_ROWS()` (query `aa03c203`) is not cached: it reads no table and returns the row count of the previous query on the same connection
risks.mitigation: Review these trade-offs with the team that builds ElastiCache before Wave 2 starts, and test each one the application depends on.

risks.description: [dynamodb] Routing did not penalise DynamoDB for the frequent-full-scan finding the source shows on 1 query, because the design removes the read it is about (each query's evidence says how).
details: A whole read of a small reference table, which the design keeps as one item collection or caches.
risks.mitigation: Design this query in DynamoDB as each one's evidence says, and serve none of them as a scan. See the Wave 3 gate in the roadmap.

mitigation_strategies: After wave 1 (Aurora MySQL): compare the latency of 163 queries with their source baseline (weighted average 1.33 ms) and check the engine sustains the collected traffic of 1,571.4 requests/s before starting wave 2.
After wave 2 (ElastiCache): track the cache hit rate for the 38 hot reads it fronts on Aurora MySQL (82.1% of calls, 1,289.4 calls/s) and compare their latency with the source before starting wave 3.
After wave 3 (DynamoDB): compare the latency of 55 queries with their source baseline (weighted average 0.76 ms) and check the engine sustains the collected traffic of 923.7 requests/s.

optimizations.recommendation: Route the WooCommerce sales report queries (`a0b655ea`, `fc99562b`, `cb3300c6`, `f86b4be6`, `d99618ea`) to an Aurora Replica through the cluster reader endpoint, and keep the storefront and admin writes on the writer endpoint.
optimizations.rationale: These report queries run about once every 3 to 8 seconds but examine up to 569,000 rows per call (query `a0b655ea` averages 1.6 s), and together they hold more database time than the 90 calls per second of postmeta lookups. Moving them to a replica keeps that scan load off the writer that serves the storefront.

optimizations.recommendation: Review query `59163c18` with `EXPLAIN` on the target: it joins `wp_actionscheduler_groups` on `slug` and filters `hook`, `status` and `claim_id`, and examines about 24,000 rows to return less than one. If the plan picks `group_id` or `status_scheduled_date_gmt`, an index on (`hook`, `group_id`, `status`) or rewriting the group filter as `a.group_id = ?` with the group id resolved first lets it read only matching rows. Purge completed and failed actions on a schedule so the table stays small.
optimizations.rationale: Query `59163c18` runs 3.2 times per second at 153 ms each and is the busiest query by total time in this design. The existing `hook_status_scheduled_date_gmt` index uses a 163-character prefix on `hook`, which does not cover the group filter.

AGAINST`. The `LIKE '%term%'` predicates the source uses cannot use any B-tree index.
optimizations.rationale: Each search call examines about 1,150 rows of `wp_posts` today. The cost grows with the table, and the search work now stays on Aurora MySQL.

optimizations.recommendation: Do not partition any table at this size. Revisit partitioning of `wp_postmeta` only if it grows past tens of millions of rows; WordPress queries it by `post_id`, so a hash partition on `post_id` is the shape to evaluate then.
optimizations.rationale: The largest table, `wp_postmeta`, holds 910,705 rows in 131 MB, which fits in the buffer pool of any production instance class. Partitioning would add a partition key to every primary and unique key without reducing reads.

trade_offs.description: Added composite indexes on (`post_id`, `meta_key`), (`user_id`, `meta_key`) and (`order_item_id`, `meta_key`) to the three metadata tables, next to the existing single-column indexes.
trade_offs.impact: The busiest point lookups (queries `3dbc7d9a`, `eb232c6c`, `22cb9563`, together about 118 calls per second) read only the matching row instead of every metadata row of the post, user or order item. Each insert and update on those tables now maintains one more index, which costs little at the write rates measured.

trade_offs.description: Added an index on `wp_posts` (`post_type`, `post_date`, `ID`) for the admin post lists that exclude statuses with `!=` and sort by date.
trade_offs.impact: Query `12f856ea` examines about 47,000 rows to return 20 because the existing `type_status_date` index cannot use a not-equal status filter. The new index reads posts of one type in date order and stops at the page size. It adds one index to maintain on each post write.

trade_offs.description: Report queries go to an Aurora Replica through the reader endpoint.
trade_offs.impact: Sales and refund reports read data up to about 100 ms behind the writer (Aurora replica lag, visible in the `AuroraReplicaLag` metric). Dashboards show figures that are at most that far behind, and the storefront keeps the writer's full capacity.

trade_offs.description: Date columns that defaulted to the MySQL zero date have no default (`NOT NULL` columns) or default to NULL (nullable Action Scheduler columns) on Aurora MySQL.
trade_offs.impact: Existing rows holding `0000-00-00 00:00:00` need a real date before or during the data load, and any code that relied on the zero-date default must write the column itself. WordPress core and WooCommerce already do.

trade_offs.description: No table is partitioned.
trade_offs.impact: All tables together are under 300 MB and the largest has 910,705 rows, so a single Aurora MySQL cluster serves them from memory. Partitioning would change primary keys without a read benefit at this size.

trade_offs.description: Posts and their meta share one item collection in the `wp_posts` table keyed by post_id: the post is the item with sort key POST and each meta row an item with sort key META#{meta_key}#{meta_id}.
trade_offs.impact: A post read by ID stays a single GetItem, and every meta row of a post sits under the same key, so the meta update by post and key (query `ea7778db` and its pattern) is a Query on one partition instead of an index lookup on a 910,705-row table.

trade_offs.description: The tables keep the source surrogate ids (post ID, comment ID, user ID) as partition keys: post_name, user_login and user_email have only non-unique indexes in the source, so none of them is proven unique enough to be a key.
trade_offs.impact: Every lookup in this workload is by ID, and other parts of the design read these rows by the same IDs, so they keep working unchanged; a duplicate post slug or login cannot overwrite another row.

trade_offs.description: The meta sort key META#{meta_key}#{meta_id} groups a post's or comment's meta by key; a NULL meta_key becomes an empty segment (META##{meta_id}), and the meta-by-comment read (query `65f7884e`) is sorted by meta_id in the application.
trade_offs.impact: Reads by key are prefix Queries; the read of all a comment's meta returns about 9 items, so the sort in application code is cheap.

trade_offs.description: The KEYS_ONLY index PostmetaByMetaId on meta_id serves the delete of post meta by meta_id (query `596b8fed`), which names no post_id; only META items carry meta_id, so post items stay out of the index.
trade_offs.impact: Each post meta insert also writes the index, about 28.5 extra write units per second, for a delete that runs 0.0114 times per second; the index lags the table until DynamoDB applies each write to it, so a meta row inserted and deleted within that window is found by a retry of the delete.

trade_offs.description: Comments and their meta share one item collection in the `wp_comments` table keyed by comment_id, with sort keys COMMENT and META#{meta_key}#{meta_id}.
trade_offs.impact: The comment meta reads, count and insert all address one comment's partition; with 6,820 meta rows over 55,500 comments, each collection holds a few items.

trade_offs.description: The comment meta count by comment and meta key (query `0278ef63`) is a Query with Select=COUNT on the comment partition and the META#{meta_key}# prefix, with no counter item.
trade_offs.impact: The count reads about one item at 0.12 requests per second, so a counter maintained on every write would cost more than it saves.

trade_offs.description: Reads by an IN list of IDs (posts, comments, users) become BatchGetItem calls of up to 100 keys, and the comment meta read by an IN list of comment IDs becomes one Query per comment run in parallel.
trade_offs.impact: The application issues the batch call, retries any UnprocessedKeys it returns, and merges the results; the lists measured here average 8 to 9 IDs.

trade_offs.description: The post read by ID and post type (query `3440484f`) is a GetItem by post_id with the post_type check done in the application.
trade_offs.impact: The read costs the same as a lookup by ID, and the dropped ORDER BY had one row to sort.

trade_offs.description: The source's AUTO_INCREMENT ids for posts, post meta, comments, comment meta and users are generated by the application, and each insert is a conditional PutItem that fails when the key already exists.
trade_offs.impact: The application needs an id source (an atomic counter item updated with ADD, or a reserved block of ids per writer); a collision makes the insert fail and retry with a new id instead of overwriting a row.

trade_offs.description: No sentinel items are written for users: the source has no unique index besides the primary key on `wp_users` (user_email and user_login are non-unique indexes), so DynamoDB enforces uniqueness on user_id only.
trade_offs.impact: Login and email uniqueness stays the WordPress application check it is in the source; two concurrent sign-ups with the same login can both succeed, as they can in the source schema.

trade_offs.description: The long text columns (post_content, post_content_filtered, post_title, post_excerpt, to_ping, pinged, comment_content and both meta_value columns) stay inline: the measured average rows are 757 bytes for posts, 446 for comments and 151 for post meta, against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: A value that would take an item past 400 KB (a very large post body or serialized meta value) is stored in Amazon S3 with a pointer attribute on the item; every other value is read in the same request as its item.

trade_offs.description: DATETIME columns become ISO 8601 strings; the source default '0000-00-00 00:00:00' has no valid ISO form and is written as an empty string.
trade_offs.impact: Dates sort as text in the same order as in the source, and code that tests for the zero date tests for the empty string instead.

trade_offs.description: Capacity uses the measured request rates (peak not measured, so the peak factor is 1) and the measured average row sizes; the busiest key load is the `wp_posts` table's 54.6 read units per second in total, spread over 24,276 posts.
trade_offs.impact: No table or index comes near the 3,000 read or 1,000 write units per second that one partition key value allows, so no sharding is needed.

trade_offs.description: The `wp_woocommerce_api_keys` table stays keyed by key_id, and the consumer-key lookup of query `1794daed` runs on the ConsumerKeyIndex GSI, because the source's consumer_key index is not unique and a table key on it would let one PutItem overwrite another key's row.
trade_offs.impact: API authentication reads an index instead of the table. ConsumerKeyIndex lags the table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a key created in the admin screen authenticates once that write reaches the index, and a flow that must see it at once reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem by key_id.

trade_offs.description: ConsumerKeyIndex uses an INCLUDE projection of user_id, permissions, consumer_secret and nonces, which covers every column query `1794daed` returns, and leaves last_access out so the 85 updates per second of query `0452bed2` never write to the index.
trade_offs.impact: Authentication needs no second read of the table, and the frequent last-access update costs 2 write units per call on the table only (about 170 write units per second in total).

trade_offs.description: The nonces LONGTEXT column of `wp_woocommerce_api_keys` stays inline as a string attribute: the table's measured avg_row_size_bytes is 52,429 against the 400 KB item limit, and the design counts the column at 1 KB.
trade_offs.impact: A nonce list that grows past 400 KB makes the write fail; the application trims old nonces before it writes the item, or moves the list to Amazon S3 with a pointer attribute if it outgrows that limit.

trade_offs.description: The unique user_id of `wp_wc_customer_lookup` is enforced with a USER_ID_SENTINEL item (USER#{user_id}) in the same item collection, written with the CUSTOMER item in one TransactWriteItems whose Put carries attribute_not_exists(customer_lookup_key) OR customer_id = :customer_id.
trade_offs.impact: Two customers can never claim one WordPress user. The upsert of queries `611079ff` and `ee8b8e21` writes 2 items (1 for a guest with no user_id, 3 when the user_id changes and the old sentinel is deleted), each billed twice as a transaction: about 6 write units per call, 7.3 write units per second in total. The transaction stays far below the 100-item limit and holds only in the Region that runs it on a global table.

trade_offs.description: The customer-by-user lookup of query `3b1641a7` is a strongly consistent GetItem on the user's sentinel item, which carries customer_id, so no GSI on user_id is needed.
trade_offs.impact: The lookup that precedes each customer upsert sees the latest mapping and costs 1 read unit per call; there is no index to keep current.

trade_offs.description: Customer items stay keyed by the surrogate customer_id (CUSTOMER#{customer_id}): the natural candidate user_id is unique but nullable, since guest customers have no WordPress account, so it cannot be the table key.
trade_offs.impact: Every customer, guest or registered, has one stable key; registered customers are also reachable by user_id through their sentinel item.

trade_offs.description: The source REPLACE INTO of queries `611079ff` and `ee8b8e21` becomes a Put of the whole CUSTOMER item, which replaces the previous version in place, inside the sentinel transaction.
trade_offs.impact: The upsert keeps its replace semantics without the delete and insert pair MySQL runs for REPLACE (which is why the source reports 1.77 affected rows per call).

trade_offs.description: The 2 tax rate classes share one constant partition key (tax_rate_class_scope = ALL) with tax_rate_class_id as the sort key, so query `329367a2` is one Query instead of a full table scan, and the application sorts the 2 items by name.
trade_offs.impact: The list read costs 0.5 read units per call (about 4.6 read units per second in total), 0.15% of one key value's limit; slug stays unique with no sentinel because no in-scope write sets it.

trade_offs.description: `wp_woocommerce_downloadable_product_permissions` is keyed order_id plus permission_id and `wp_wc_reserved_stock` order_id plus product_id, so the key-scoped writes of queries `2264704d` and `77cd1ad7` find their items with a Query on order_id and then update or delete each item by key.
trade_offs.impact: Neither write scans its table; each costs one Query plus one write per matching item. A read of a download permission by permission_id alone has no key in this design and needs a GSI on permission_id if one is added later.

trade_offs.description: The auto-increment ids log_id, customer_id, key_id and permission_id are generated by the application, and the log insert of query `b05af520` carries attribute_not_exists(log_id) so a reused id fails instead of overwriting a log entry.
trade_offs.impact: The application needs an id source (for example a counter item updated with an atomic ADD, or a time-ordered id) in place of MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT.

trade_offs.description: The message TEXT column of `wp_actionscheduler_logs` stays inline: the table's measured avg_row_size_bytes is 182 against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: Each log entry is one item written for 2 write units at the schema's 1,188-byte size estimate; a message over 400 KB fails the write.

trade_offs.description: DATETIME and TIMESTAMP columns become ISO 8601 strings, and the MySQL zero date '0000-00-00 00:00:00' is written as an absent attribute.
trade_offs.impact: Dates sort correctly as strings; code that tested for the zero date tests for a missing attribute instead.

trade_offs.description: Order item meta rows are stored in the same item collection as their order item, keyed by order_item_id with sort keys ITEM and META#{meta_id}, because every meta write in scope (queries `2caa2be1` and `4b856e29`) addresses meta by order_item_id.
trade_offs.impact: One Query on an order item returns the item and its meta (about 9 meta rows per item: 473,830 meta rows over 48,460 items); a meta update reads that collection, filters on meta_key and updates each match by its key.

trade_offs.description: Term meta is keyed by term_id with meta_id as the sort key, and the KEYS_ONLY index TermMetaByTermAndKey (partition key term_id and meta_key, sort key meta_id) serves the meta_id lookup (query `ee386e4a`) and finds the items the key-scoped update (query `3c5c8a79`) changes.
trade_offs.impact: Reading a term's meta in meta_id order (query `50b46567`) is one Query per term id in the IN list instead of the full table scans the source ran; the index returns only keys, so the lookup reads no base item and the update writes nothing to the index, because meta_value is not one of its keys.

trade_offs.description: TermMetaByTermAndKey lags the wp_termmeta table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a caller that must see a meta row written in the same request reads the term's base items with a strongly consistent Query on term_id.
trade_offs.impact: The meta_id lookup and the update's item search read the index eventually consistent, which matches the source workload: no term meta insert runs in this part of the workload.

trade_offs.description: User meta updates by user_id and meta_key (query `41b2f2d1`) are a Query on the user's partition with a filter on meta_key, then an UpdateItem per match, with no secondary index.
trade_offs.impact: A user has about 19 meta rows (the source examines 18.8 per update) at 144 bytes each, so the Query reads under 4 KB, half a read unit, and an index on meta_key would add a write to every one of the 8.4 inserts per second.

trade_offs.description: The auto-increment ids action_id, umeta_id, order_item_id and meta_id of order item meta are generated by the application on insert, and each new item's PutItem is conditional on the id not existing where a duplicate would overwrite a row.
trade_offs.impact: Your application needs an id generator (a counter item updated with an atomic ADD, or a Snowflake-style id) that keeps ids numeric and increasing, because the term meta, user meta and order item meta reads sort by them.

trade_offs.description: Every table keeps the source's surrogate id in its key: no natural attribute in this part qualifies, since sku in wp_wc_product_meta_lookup is nullable and not unique, and the unique (term_id, taxonomy) pair of wp_term_taxonomy is not what its queries look up by (they read by term_taxonomy_id).
trade_offs.impact: Other parts of the design that read these rows by their source id reach them with GetItem or Query on the same key; no unique attribute is inserted or changed by a write here, so no sentinel item is needed (the term count update leaves term_id and taxonomy unchanged).

trade_offs.description: The scheduled-action insert (query `7ead756f`) is an INSERT ... SELECT guarded by a subquery that tests only a bound value, so the application evaluates that guard and then writes a PutItem conditional on attribute_not_exists(action_id).
trade_offs.impact: The write stays a single-item PutItem; the source table's status and date indexes have no in-scope reader here, so no secondary index is created for them in this table.

trade_offs.description: Large text columns stay inline: meta_value in wp_usermeta (144-byte average row) and in wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta (139 bytes), order_item_name (131 bytes), description in wp_term_taxonomy (3,495 bytes) and schedule and extended_args in wp_actionscheduler_actions (706 bytes) are all far below the 400 KB item limit; wp_termmeta has no rows to measure.
trade_offs.impact: A single value above 400 KB fails its PutItem; the application stores such a value in Amazon S3 with a pointer attribute in the item.

trade_offs.description: REPLACE INTO wp_wc_product_meta_lookup (query `d72966f8`) becomes an unconditional PutItem on product_id, which replaces the whole item in one write where MySQL deletes and reinserts the row.
trade_offs.impact: The write costs one write unit per call at 618 bytes per item, and every PutItem carries all fourteen columns, as the source statement does.

trade_offs.description: The wp_options table is keyed on option_name instead of the surrogate option_id, because every in-scope read and write addresses an option by its name and option_name is unique, NOT NULL and has one distinct value per row (55,527).
trade_offs.impact: Lookups, updates, upserts and deletes are single-item calls on the table key, and DynamoDB enforces one item per option name without a sentinel; renaming an option is a delete and a put, which WordPress never does in the captured workload.

trade_offs.description: The source primary key option_id stays reachable through the KEYS_ONLY index OptionsById, so another part of the design that reads an option by its id finds its option_name with one Query and then reads the item.
trade_offs.impact: The index adds one small write (about 60 bytes) when an option is created or deleted, 12.80 write units per second at most; value updates do not touch it because option_id never changes.

trade_offs.description: MySQL generated option_id with AUTO_INCREMENT; the application now generates it as a 64-bit time-ordered id (timestamp, worker and sequence bits) and writes it with if_not_exists(option_id, :new_id) in the upsert, so an existing option keeps its id.
trade_offs.impact: Ids are unique by construction and are never reused, so no sentinel item guards them; they are no longer consecutive, which no captured query relies on.

trade_offs.description: The autoload read (query `413c99e4`) is served by the OptionsByAutoload index, partitioned on autoload with option_name as sort key and option_value projected, so one Query returns the about 249 autoloaded options without a Scan or a base-table fetch.
trade_offs.impact: autoload has few distinct values, so each value is one index partition: the read is 101.08 read units per second and the index writes 37.18 write units per second at design load, both under 4% of one partition key value's limit, so no shard suffix is needed. Every option write also writes the index (twice when the upsert changes autoload).

trade_offs.description: OptionsByAutoload lags the wp_options table until DynamoDB applies each write to it, so the autoload Query can return an option's previous value; a caller that must see the latest value reads the item with a strongly consistent GetItem on option_name.
trade_offs.impact: Per-option reads by name stay current when read strongly consistent at 1 read unit per item instead of 0.5; the update returns the new item with ReturnValues=ALL_NEW, so a read right after a write needs no extra call.

trade_offs.description: option_value (LONGTEXT) stays inline in the item: the table's average row is 338 bytes against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: A write whose value exceeds 400 KB is rejected by DynamoDB; the application stores such a value in Amazon S3 and keeps the object key in option_value with a marker, and reads it from S3 when the marker is present.

trade_offs.description: The UPDATE by option_name carries attribute_exists(option_name), so it changes only an option that exists, as the SQL UPDATE does, while the INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE becomes an unconditional UpdateItem that creates or overwrites.
trade_offs.impact: An update of a missing option (most of the 71% of updates that change no row in the source) fails with a conditional check error that the application treats as zero rows affected; a failed conditional write still consumes one write unit.

trade_offs.description: Each metadata table (post, user, order item, term, comment meta) is cached as one JSON array per parent id, read in full and deleted in full on any write to that parent.
trade_offs.impact: A post's 26 meta rows come back in one round trip, matching how WordPress loads them, and a single meta write deletes the whole array, so the next read refills it from the owner database.

trade_offs.description: Every cached key is cleared by the application after the owner write commits, and every key carries a TTL as the fallback bound.
trade_offs.impact: After a write the cached value stays until the application deletes its key, and for at most its TTL (60 seconds for scheduled actions, 10 to 15 minutes for orders, users and child post lists, one hour for options, posts, terms and comments) if that delete fails. A read that must see the write before then reads the owner database, which serves every cache miss.

trade_offs.description: The object-to-terms joins are denormalized into one array per object and taxonomy, holding each term's id and name in name order.
trade_offs.impact: The three-table join that runs about 80 times a second becomes one key read per object and taxonomy. A term rename has no captured write, so a cached array shows the old name order for at most the one-hour TTL unless the admin edit deletes the taxonomy keys.

trade_offs.description: IN-list queries (posts, post meta, user meta, order item meta, terms, comment meta) become one pipelined `GET` per id, because the per-entity hash tags put the ids in different slots.
trade_offs.impact: A list of nine posts is one network round trip of nine commands. A single `MGET` across those keys is refused with a `CROSSSLOT` error in cluster mode, so the client library pipelines them instead.

trade_offs.description: Lookups that return no row in most calls (option names at 0.31 rows a call, post titles and child posts at zero, post meta existence at 0.04) cache a miss marker with a 300-second TTL.
trade_offs.impact: Repeated lookups for missing options and posts stop reaching the owner database. A row created on the owner shows for these lookups when the write's invalidation deletes the marker, and for at most 300 seconds if that delete fails.

trade_offs.description: The cached user rows hold password hashes and activation keys, and cached user meta holds session tokens, because the source queries return every column.
trade_offs.impact: The cache holds credential material, so it runs with encryption in transit and at rest and with access control (IAM authentication or user access strings) limited to the application.

trade_offs.description: The slug check before a post save (query `fcfd82fa`) and the pending-action check before an action is scheduled (query `06584926`) are served from the cache, with the insert that changes each answer deleting its key.
trade_offs.impact: A post or action inserted on the owner shows in these checks once the write's invalidation deletes the key. The check and the insert are separate statements on the owner database too, so two concurrent saves can pass the same check there as well. Status updates by the queue runner are not in the captured writes, so the pending-action list lags them for at most its 30-second TTL; code that needs the committed answer reads the owner database.

trade_offs.description: The related-products query (query `4b79d7a8`) is cached as its result list, keyed by a digest of its parameters, with expiry as its only invalidation.
trade_offs.impact: Its result depends on the term links of every candidate post, and no single write names the cached lists it changes, so a related-products list reflects term and status changes after at most its one-hour TTL.

trade_offs.description: `FOUND_ROWS()` (query `aa03c203`) is not cached: it reads no table and returns the row count of the previous query on the same connection.
trade_offs.impact: The call stays on the owner database. When the child id list of `EC-AP-22` comes from the cache, the application takes the total from that array's length and skips this call.

trade_offs.description: The cached working set is about 300 MB across about 500,000 keys at full fill, the largest being post rows (about 100 MB) and post meta arrays (about 63 MB).
trade_offs.impact: The set fits the planned cache with room to spare, and per-entity hash tags spread the hottest key families (options at about 529 reads a second) across slots, so no slot nears its throughput limit.

unsupported_patterns.reason: Query `aa03c203` (`FOUND_ROWS()`) reads no table: it returns the row count of the previous `SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS` query on the same database connection, so it has no cacheable key.
unsupported_patterns.workaround: The query stays on its owner database. When the child id list of `EC-AP-22` comes from the cache, the application takes the total from that array's length and skips this call.

migration_notes.application_logic_required: Every read tries the cache first and, on a miss, reads the owner database and fills the key with its TTL. Lookups that most calls answer with no row (options, post titles, child posts, customer ids) store a miss marker with a 300-second TTL so repeated misses stay off the owner.
After each owner write listed in the cache invalidation section commits, the application deletes the listed keys. Keys of one entity share a hash tag, so one `DEL` clears them in one call.

Hashes and sets that answer existence checks are filled whole from the owner with a `_loaded` field or a `0` member, and the application treats a missing field or member in a loaded key as a definite no and a missing key as a cache miss.

trade_offs.description: Added composite indexes on (`post_id`, `meta_key`), (`user_id`, `meta_key`) and (`order_item_id`, `meta_key`) to the three metadata tables, next to the existing single-column indexes.
trade_offs.impact: The busiest point lookups (queries `3dbc7d9a`, `eb232c6c`, `22cb9563`, together about 118 calls per second) read only the matching row instead of every metadata row of the post, user or order item. Each insert and update on those tables now maintains one more index, which costs little at the write rates measured.

trade_offs.description: Added an index on `wp_posts` (`post_type`, `post_date`, `ID`) for the admin post lists that exclude statuses with `!=` and sort by date.
trade_offs.impact: Query `12f856ea` examines about 47,000 rows to return 20 because the existing `type_status_date` index cannot use a not-equal status filter. The new index reads posts of one type in date order and stops at the page size. It adds one index to maintain on each post write.

trade_offs.description: Report queries go to an Aurora Replica through the reader endpoint.
trade_offs.impact: Sales and refund reports read data up to about 100 ms behind the writer (Aurora replica lag, visible in the `AuroraReplicaLag` metric). Dashboards show figures that are at most that far behind, and the storefront keeps the writer's full capacity.

trade_offs.description: Date columns that defaulted to the MySQL zero date have no default (`NOT NULL` columns) or default to NULL (nullable Action Scheduler columns) on Aurora MySQL.
trade_offs.impact: Existing rows holding `0000-00-00 00:00:00` need a real date before or during the data load, and any code that relied on the zero-date default must write the column itself. WordPress core and WooCommerce already do.

trade_offs.description: No table is partitioned.
trade_offs.impact: All tables together are under 300 MB and the largest has 910,705 rows, so a single Aurora MySQL cluster serves them from memory. Partitioning would change primary keys without a read benefit at this size.

trade_offs.description: Posts and their meta share one item collection in the `wp_posts` table keyed by post_id: the post is the item with sort key POST and each meta row an item with sort key META#{meta_key}#{meta_id}.
trade_offs.impact: A post read by ID stays a single GetItem, and every meta row of a post sits under the same key, so the meta update by post and key (query `ea7778db` and its pattern) is a Query on one partition instead of an index lookup on a 910,705-row table.

trade_offs.description: The tables keep the source surrogate ids (post ID, comment ID, user ID) as partition keys: post_name, user_login and user_email have only non-unique indexes in the source, so none of them is proven unique enough to be a key.
trade_offs.impact: Every lookup in this workload is by ID, and other parts of the design read these rows by the same IDs, so they keep working unchanged; a duplicate post slug or login cannot overwrite another row.

trade_offs.description: The meta sort key META#{meta_key}#{meta_id} groups a post's or comment's meta by key; a NULL meta_key becomes an empty segment (META##{meta_id}), and the meta-by-comment read (query `65f7884e`) is sorted by meta_id in the application.
trade_offs.impact: Reads by key are prefix Queries; the read of all a comment's meta returns about 9 items, so the sort in application code is cheap.

trade_offs.description: The KEYS_ONLY index PostmetaByMetaId on meta_id serves the delete of post meta by meta_id (query `596b8fed`), which names no post_id; only META items carry meta_id, so post items stay out of the index.
trade_offs.impact: Each post meta insert also writes the index, about 28.5 extra write units per second, for a delete that runs 0.0114 times per second; the index lags the table until DynamoDB applies each write to it, so a meta row inserted and deleted within that window is found by a retry of the delete.

trade_offs.description: Comments and their meta share one item collection in the `wp_comments` table keyed by comment_id, with sort keys COMMENT and META#{meta_key}#{meta_id}.
trade_offs.impact: The comment meta reads, count and insert all address one comment's partition; with 6,820 meta rows over 55,500 comments, each collection holds a few items.

trade_offs.description: The comment meta count by comment and meta key (query `0278ef63`) is a Query with Select=COUNT on the comment partition and the META#{meta_key}# prefix, with no counter item.
trade_offs.impact: The count reads about one item at 0.12 requests per second, so a counter maintained on every write would cost more than it saves.

trade_offs.description: Reads by an IN list of IDs (posts, comments, users) become BatchGetItem calls of up to 100 keys, and the comment meta read by an IN list of comment IDs becomes one Query per comment run in parallel.
trade_offs.impact: The application issues the batch call, retries any UnprocessedKeys it returns, and merges the results; the lists measured here average 8 to 9 IDs.

trade_offs.description: The post read by ID and post type (query `3440484f`) is a GetItem by post_id with the post_type check done in the application.
trade_offs.impact: The read costs the same as a lookup by ID, and the dropped ORDER BY had one row to sort.

trade_offs.description: The source's AUTO_INCREMENT ids for posts, post meta, comments, comment meta and users are generated by the application, and each insert is a conditional PutItem that fails when the key already exists.
trade_offs.impact: The application needs an id source (an atomic counter item updated with ADD, or a reserved block of ids per writer); a collision makes the insert fail and retry with a new id instead of overwriting a row.

trade_offs.description: No sentinel items are written for users: the source has no unique index besides the primary key on `wp_users` (user_email and user_login are non-unique indexes), so DynamoDB enforces uniqueness on user_id only.
trade_offs.impact: Login and email uniqueness stays the WordPress application check it is in the source; two concurrent sign-ups with the same login can both succeed, as they can in the source schema.

trade_offs.description: The long text columns (post_content, post_content_filtered, post_title, post_excerpt, to_ping, pinged, comment_content and both meta_value columns) stay inline: the measured average rows are 757 bytes for posts, 446 for comments and 151 for post meta, against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: A value that would take an item past 400 KB (a very large post body or serialized meta value) is stored in Amazon S3 with a pointer attribute on the item; every other value is read in the same request as its item.

trade_offs.description: DATETIME columns become ISO 8601 strings; the source default '0000-00-00 00:00:00' has no valid ISO form and is written as an empty string.
trade_offs.impact: Dates sort as text in the same order as in the source, and code that tests for the zero date tests for the empty string instead.

trade_offs.description: Capacity uses the measured request rates (peak not measured, so the peak factor is 1) and the measured average row sizes; the busiest key load is the `wp_posts` table's 54.6 read units per second in total, spread over 24,276 posts.
trade_offs.impact: No table or index comes near the 3,000 read or 1,000 write units per second that one partition key value allows, so no sharding is needed.

trade_offs.description: The `wp_woocommerce_api_keys` table stays keyed by key_id, and the consumer-key lookup of query `1794daed` runs on the ConsumerKeyIndex GSI, because the source's consumer_key index is not unique and a table key on it would let one PutItem overwrite another key's row.
trade_offs.impact: API authentication reads an index instead of the table. ConsumerKeyIndex lags the table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a key created in the admin screen authenticates once that write reaches the index, and a flow that must see it at once reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem by key_id.

trade_offs.description: ConsumerKeyIndex uses an INCLUDE projection of user_id, permissions, consumer_secret and nonces, which covers every column query `1794daed` returns, and leaves last_access out so the 85 updates per second of query `0452bed2` never write to the index.
trade_offs.impact: Authentication needs no second read of the table, and the frequent last-access update costs 2 write units per call on the table only (about 170 write units per second in total).

trade_offs.description: The nonces LONGTEXT column of `wp_woocommerce_api_keys` stays inline as a string attribute: the table's measured avg_row_size_bytes is 52,429 against the 400 KB item limit, and the design counts the column at 1 KB.
trade_offs.impact: A nonce list that grows past 400 KB makes the write fail; the application trims old nonces before it writes the item, or moves the list to Amazon S3 with a pointer attribute if it outgrows that limit.

trade_offs.description: The unique user_id of `wp_wc_customer_lookup` is enforced with a USER_ID_SENTINEL item (USER#{user_id}) in the same item collection, written with the CUSTOMER item in one TransactWriteItems whose Put carries attribute_not_exists(customer_lookup_key) OR customer_id = :customer_id.
trade_offs.impact: Two customers can never claim one WordPress user. The upsert of queries `611079ff` and `ee8b8e21` writes 2 items (1 for a guest with no user_id, 3 when the user_id changes and the old sentinel is deleted), each billed twice as a transaction: about 6 write units per call, 7.3 write units per second in total. The transaction stays far below the 100-item limit and holds only in the Region that runs it on a global table.

trade_offs.description: The customer-by-user lookup of query `3b1641a7` is a strongly consistent GetItem on the user's sentinel item, which carries customer_id, so no GSI on user_id is needed.
trade_offs.impact: The lookup that precedes each customer upsert sees the latest mapping and costs 1 read unit per call; there is no index to keep current.

trade_offs.description: Customer items stay keyed by the surrogate customer_id (CUSTOMER#{customer_id}): the natural candidate user_id is unique but nullable, since guest customers have no WordPress account, so it cannot be the table key.
trade_offs.impact: Every customer, guest or registered, has one stable key; registered customers are also reachable by user_id through their sentinel item.

trade_offs.description: The source REPLACE INTO of queries `611079ff` and `ee8b8e21` becomes a Put of the whole CUSTOMER item, which replaces the previous version in place, inside the sentinel transaction.
trade_offs.impact: The upsert keeps its replace semantics without the delete and insert pair MySQL runs for REPLACE (which is why the source reports 1.77 affected rows per call).

trade_offs.description: The 2 tax rate classes share one constant partition key (tax_rate_class_scope = ALL) with tax_rate_class_id as the sort key, so query `329367a2` is one Query instead of a full table scan, and the application sorts the 2 items by name.
trade_offs.impact: The list read costs 0.5 read units per call (about 4.6 read units per second in total), 0.15% of one key value's limit; slug stays unique with no sentinel because no in-scope write sets it.

trade_offs.description: `wp_woocommerce_downloadable_product_permissions` is keyed order_id plus permission_id and `wp_wc_reserved_stock` order_id plus product_id, so the key-scoped writes of queries `2264704d` and `77cd1ad7` find their items with a Query on order_id and then update or delete each item by key.
trade_offs.impact: Neither write scans its table; each costs one Query plus one write per matching item. A read of a download permission by permission_id alone has no key in this design and needs a GSI on permission_id if one is added later.

trade_offs.description: The auto-increment ids log_id, customer_id, key_id and permission_id are generated by the application, and the log insert of query `b05af520` carries attribute_not_exists(log_id) so a reused id fails instead of overwriting a log entry.
trade_offs.impact: The application needs an id source (for example a counter item updated with an atomic ADD, or a time-ordered id) in place of MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT.

trade_offs.description: The message TEXT column of `wp_actionscheduler_logs` stays inline: the table's measured avg_row_size_bytes is 182 against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: Each log entry is one item written for 2 write units at the schema's 1,188-byte size estimate; a message over 400 KB fails the write.

trade_offs.description: DATETIME and TIMESTAMP columns become ISO 8601 strings, and the MySQL zero date '0000-00-00 00:00:00' is written as an absent attribute.
trade_offs.impact: Dates sort correctly as strings; code that tested for the zero date tests for a missing attribute instead.

trade_offs.description: Order item meta rows are stored in the same item collection as their order item, keyed by order_item_id with sort keys ITEM and META#{meta_id}, because every meta write in scope (queries `2caa2be1` and `4b856e29`) addresses meta by order_item_id.
trade_offs.impact: One Query on an order item returns the item and its meta (about 9 meta rows per item: 473,830 meta rows over 48,460 items); a meta update reads that collection, filters on meta_key and updates each match by its key.

trade_offs.description: Term meta is keyed by term_id with meta_id as the sort key, and the KEYS_ONLY index TermMetaByTermAndKey (partition key term_id and meta_key, sort key meta_id) serves the meta_id lookup (query `ee386e4a`) and finds the items the key-scoped update (query `3c5c8a79`) changes.
trade_offs.impact: Reading a term's meta in meta_id order (query `50b46567`) is one Query per term id in the IN list instead of the full table scans the source ran; the index returns only keys, so the lookup reads no base item and the update writes nothing to the index, because meta_value is not one of its keys.

trade_offs.description: TermMetaByTermAndKey lags the wp_termmeta table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a caller that must see a meta row written in the same request reads the term's base items with a strongly consistent Query on term_id.
trade_offs.impact: The meta_id lookup and the update's item search read the index eventually consistent, which matches the source workload: no term meta insert runs in this part of the workload.

trade_offs.description: User meta updates by user_id and meta_key (query `41b2f2d1`) are a Query on the user's partition with a filter on meta_key, then an UpdateItem per match, with no secondary index.
trade_offs.impact: A user has about 19 meta rows (the source examines 18.8 per update) at 144 bytes each, so the Query reads under 4 KB, half a read unit, and an index on meta_key would add a write to every one of the 8.4 inserts per second.

trade_offs.description: The auto-increment ids action_id, umeta_id, order_item_id and meta_id of order item meta are generated by the application on insert, and each new item's PutItem is conditional on the id not existing where a duplicate would overwrite a row.
trade_offs.impact: Your application needs an id generator (a counter item updated with an atomic ADD, or a Snowflake-style id) that keeps ids numeric and increasing, because the term meta, user meta and order item meta reads sort by them.

trade_offs.description: Every table keeps the source's surrogate id in its key: no natural attribute in this part qualifies, since sku in wp_wc_product_meta_lookup is nullable and not unique, and the unique (term_id, taxonomy) pair of wp_term_taxonomy is not what its queries look up by (they read by term_taxonomy_id).
trade_offs.impact: Other parts of the design that read these rows by their source id reach them with GetItem or Query on the same key; no unique attribute is inserted or changed by a write here, so no sentinel item is needed (the term count update leaves term_id and taxonomy unchanged).

trade_offs.description: The scheduled-action insert (query `7ead756f`) is an INSERT ... SELECT guarded by a subquery that tests only a bound value, so the application evaluates that guard and then writes a PutItem conditional on attribute_not_exists(action_id).
trade_offs.impact: The write stays a single-item PutItem; the source table's status and date indexes have no in-scope reader here, so no secondary index is created for them in this table.

trade_offs.description: Large text columns stay inline: meta_value in wp_usermeta (144-byte average row) and in wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta (139 bytes), order_item_name (131 bytes), description in wp_term_taxonomy (3,495 bytes) and schedule and extended_args in wp_actionscheduler_actions (706 bytes) are all far below the 400 KB item limit; wp_termmeta has no rows to measure.
trade_offs.impact: A single value above 400 KB fails its PutItem; the application stores such a value in Amazon S3 with a pointer attribute in the item.

trade_offs.description: REPLACE INTO wp_wc_product_meta_lookup (query `d72966f8`) becomes an unconditional PutItem on product_id, which replaces the whole item in one write where MySQL deletes and reinserts the row.
trade_offs.impact: The write costs one write unit per call at 618 bytes per item, and every PutItem carries all fourteen columns, as the source statement does.

trade_offs.description: The wp_options table is keyed on option_name instead of the surrogate option_id, because every in-scope read and write addresses an option by its name and option_name is unique, NOT NULL and has one distinct value per row (55,527).
trade_offs.impact: Lookups, updates, upserts and deletes are single-item calls on the table key, and DynamoDB enforces one item per option name without a sentinel; renaming an option is a delete and a put, which WordPress never does in the captured workload.

trade_offs.description: The source primary key option_id stays reachable through the KEYS_ONLY index OptionsById, so another part of the design that reads an option by its id finds its option_name with one Query and then reads the item.
trade_offs.impact: The index adds one small write (about 60 bytes) when an option is created or deleted, 12.80 write units per second at most; value updates do not touch it because option_id never changes.

trade_offs.description: MySQL generated option_id with AUTO_INCREMENT; the application now generates it as a 64-bit time-ordered id (timestamp, worker and sequence bits) and writes it with if_not_exists(option_id, :new_id) in the upsert, so an existing option keeps its id.
trade_offs.impact: Ids are unique by construction and are never reused, so no sentinel item guards them; they are no longer consecutive, which no captured query relies on.

trade_offs.description: The autoload read (query `413c99e4`) is served by the OptionsByAutoload index, partitioned on autoload with option_name as sort key and option_value projected, so one Query returns the about 249 autoloaded options without a Scan or a base-table fetch.
trade_offs.impact: autoload has few distinct values, so each value is one index partition: the read is 101.08 read units per second and the index writes 37.18 write units per second at design load, both under 4% of one partition key value's limit, so no shard suffix is needed. Every option write also writes the index (twice when the upsert changes autoload).

trade_offs.description: OptionsByAutoload lags the wp_options table until DynamoDB applies each write to it, so the autoload Query can return an option's previous value; a caller that must see the latest value reads the item with a strongly consistent GetItem on option_name.
trade_offs.impact: Per-option reads by name stay current when read strongly consistent at 1 read unit per item instead of 0.5; the update returns the new item with ReturnValues=ALL_NEW, so a read right after a write needs no extra call.

trade_offs.description: option_value (LONGTEXT) stays inline in the item: the table's average row is 338 bytes against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: A write whose value exceeds 400 KB is rejected by DynamoDB; the application stores such a value in Amazon S3 and keeps the object key in option_value with a marker, and reads it from S3 when the marker is present.

trade_offs.description: The UPDATE by option_name carries attribute_exists(option_name), so it changes only an option that exists, as the SQL UPDATE does, while the INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE becomes an unconditional UpdateItem that creates or overwrites.
trade_offs.impact: An update of a missing option (most of the 71% of updates that change no row in the source) fails with a conditional check error that the application treats as zero rows affected; a failed conditional write still consumes one write unit.

trade_offs.description: Each metadata table (post, user, order item, term, comment meta) is cached as one JSON array per parent id, read in full and deleted in full on any write to that parent.
trade_offs.impact: A post's 26 meta rows come back in one round trip, matching how WordPress loads them, and a single meta write deletes the whole array, so the next read refills it from the owner database.

trade_offs.description: Every cached key is cleared by the application after the owner write commits, and every key carries a TTL as the fallback bound.
trade_offs.impact: After a write the cached value stays until the application deletes its key, and for at most its TTL (60 seconds for scheduled actions, 10 to 15 minutes for orders, users and child post lists, one hour for options, posts, terms and comments) if that delete fails. A read that must see the write before then reads the owner database, which serves every cache miss.

trade_offs.description: The object-to-terms joins are denormalized into one array per object and taxonomy, holding each term's id and name in name order.
trade_offs.impact: The three-table join that runs about 80 times a second becomes one key read per object and taxonomy. A term rename has no captured write, so a cached array shows the old name order for at most the one-hour TTL unless the admin edit deletes the taxonomy keys.

trade_offs.description: IN-list queries (posts, post meta, user meta, order item meta, terms, comment meta) become one pipelined `GET` per id, because the per-entity hash tags put the ids in different slots.
trade_offs.impact: A list of nine posts is one network round trip of nine commands. A single `MGET` across those keys is refused with a `CROSSSLOT` error in cluster mode, so the client library pipelines them instead.

trade_offs.description: Lookups that return no row in most calls (option names at 0.31 rows a call, post titles and child posts at zero, post meta existence at 0.04) cache a miss marker with a 300-second TTL.
trade_offs.impact: Repeated lookups for missing options and posts stop reaching the owner database. A row created on the owner shows for these lookups when the write's invalidation deletes the marker, and for at most 300 seconds if that delete fails.

trade_offs.description: The cached user rows hold password hashes and activation keys, and cached user meta holds session tokens, because the source queries return every column.
trade_offs.impact: The cache holds credential material, so it runs with encryption in transit and at rest and with access control (IAM authentication or user access strings) limited to the application.

trade_offs.description: The slug check before a post save (query `fcfd82fa`) and the pending-action check before an action is scheduled (query `06584926`) are served from the cache, with the insert that changes each answer deleting its key.
trade_offs.impact: A post or action inserted on the owner shows in these checks once the write's invalidation deletes the key. The check and the insert are separate statements on the owner database too, so two concurrent saves can pass the same check there as well. Status updates by the queue runner are not in the captured writes, so the pending-action list lags them for at most its 30-second TTL; code that needs the committed answer reads the owner database.

trade_offs.description: The related-products query (query `4b79d7a8`) is cached as its result list, keyed by a digest of its parameters, with expiry as its only invalidation.
trade_offs.impact: Its result depends on the term links of every candidate post, and no single write names the cached lists it changes, so a related-products list reflects term and status changes after at most its one-hour TTL.

trade_offs.description: `FOUND_ROWS()` (query `aa03c203`) is not cached: it reads no table and returns the row count of the previous query on the same connection.
trade_offs.impact: The call stays on the owner database. When the child id list of `EC-AP-22` comes from the cache, the application takes the total from that array's length and skips this call.

trade_offs.description: The cached working set is about 300 MB across about 500,000 keys at full fill, the largest being post rows (about 100 MB) and post meta arrays (about 63 MB).
trade_offs.impact: The set fits the planned cache with room to spare, and per-entity hash tags spread the hottest key families (options at about 529 reads a second) across slots, so no slot nears its throughput limit.

cache_layer.role_sentence: ElastiCache is recommended as a cache-aside layer in front of the engine that owns each cached read: the cached reads are hot, small and can be rebuilt from that engine, so it stays the system of record and the cache is sized for the hot reads, not the whole dataset.
